column1: # spec: guard-kit/SPEC.md §Testing — rule `background_no_record`'s harness arm: the backgrounding flag is tool
# input, not command text, so it cannot be written in cases.tsv's decision/command grammar.
# rule `background_no_record` — a backgrounded launch that records no producer is blocked. The
#           non-firing cases are the load-bearing ones: an inline record
#           discharges the obligation, a wait loop is a waiter rather than a
#           producer, a read-only pipeline owns nothing a commit could corrupt,
#           and a foreground call never reaches the rule at all. The wait-loop
#           row is an `allow` rather than a `fallthrough` because rule `bounded_wait` grants
#           it two rules later, which still proves rule `background_no_record`'s exemption: a block
#           It is also where rule `bounded_wait`'s indifference to the harness flag is pinned
#           — the flag backgrounds the call without changing its text, so clause

column3: bash worker.sh
bash worker.sh > .tmp/worker.log 2>&1 & printf 'pid=1 run=worker\n' > .tmp/worker.run
until grep -q DONE .tmp/worker.log; do sleep 5; done
grep -rn foo src | head

column1: # exemption (3) reads `>&` onto a named file as the write `>` is, and an fd-dup spelled apart as inert

column3: grep -rn foo src > found.txt
grep -rn foo src >& found.txt
grep -rn foo src | head >&found.txt
grep -rn foo src 2>& 1
bash worker.sh

column1: # the canonical launch in harness form: rule `background_no_record`'s exemption (1) lets the record
# through and rule `bounded_wait`'s arm (B) grants it, the flag changing nothing in its text

column3: bash scripts/check-foo.sh > .tmp/foo.log 2>&1 & echo "pid=$! run=foo" > .tmp/foo.run; wait; rm -f .tmp/foo.run

column1: # exemption (2) holds only where the call does no work its text shows: every span's body only
# sleeps, whatever its keyword, and a statement outside a loop, ahead of the first or after it, is
# another such loop or only reads. A loop that works, a nest, a producer or a declared write form
# ahead of the loop or after it, and a statement other than a loop ending in a bare `&` each take
# the record. The `&` rows and the lead rows wait on a `grep`, since rule `wait_no_producer` reads
# their shell-test spelling. A body `sleep` redirecting to a named file writes, where an inert
# target does not, and a tail statement behind the loop's own `&` is read as one behind `;`.
# A condition is held to the writes its text shows, a redirect to a named file, a statement-ending
# `&` and a declared write form, and not to the read-only roster: a command outside it stays exempt.
# A loop opens at a keyword leading a statement, so `echo for` hides no lead.

for f in a b; do make build; done
while true; do until [ -f .tmp/a ]; do sleep 1; done; done
until grep -q DONE .tmp/worker.log; do sleep 5; done; make build
until grep -q DONE .tmp/worker.log; do sleep 5; done; sort -o out.txt .tmp/worker.log
until grep -q DONE .tmp/worker.log; do sleep 5 & make build; done
until grep -q DONE .tmp/worker.log; do sleep 5; done; echo waited & make build
until grep -q DONE .tmp/worker.log; do sleep 1 > out.txt; done
until grep -q DONE .tmp/worker.log; do sleep 5 2>/dev/null; done
until grep -q DONE .tmp/worker.log; do sleep 5; done & sort -o out.txt .tmp/worker.log
until grep -q DONE .tmp/worker.log; do sleep 5; done & grep -n ERR .tmp/worker.log
until grep -q DONE .tmp/worker.log; do sleep 5; done; echo waited
until grep -q DONE .tmp/worker.log; do sleep 5; done; grep -n ERR .tmp/worker.log

column1: # rule `wait_no_producer` — a backgrounded wait on a file condition is blocked while no record
#           names a live producer; the sandbox's one record names a dead pid, so
#           clause (d) holds on every row and the record-set pair is the bespoke
#           not read. The non-firing rows are one per remaining clause: a
#           foreground call, a second loop span, a condition segment that is no
#           shell test (`kill -0`, and a test joined to a command), and a body
#           that runs something besides sleep. That last loop takes rule
#           `background_no_record`'s block unrecorded, so its row launches it with its
#           record, in the spelling that block prints, and meets no second block.

column3: until [ -f .tmp/marker ]; do sleep 30; done

until test -d .tmp/out && [[ -s .tmp/out/done ]]; do sleep 30; done; echo waited
until [ -f .tmp/marker ]; do sleep 30; done; echo done
until [ -f .tmp/marker ]; do sleep 30; done | cat
until [ -f .tmp/marker ]; do sleep 30; done|cat
